e.etymology: An elaboration that reads as Lily with the -eth ending of Elizabeth, or as a softened spelling of Lilith. Its source as a given name is not documented.
From Terentius, a Roman family name of obscure origin borne by the comic playwright Terence and by early saints. In Ireland it was used as an English stand-in for the Gaelic name Turlough.
namesakes: Terence Stamp (actor, General Zod in Superman II)

e.etymology: A variant spelling of Brandon, an English place name and surname from Old English brom, 'broom shrub', and dun, 'hill'. The -en ending echoes Brendan, an unrelated Irish saint's name.

e.meaning: young attendant at religious rites (from Camilla)
e.etymology: Short form of Camilla and Camille, from the Roman family name Camillus, traditionally linked to the word for a youth who assisted at religious rites. Also spelled Cammy and Cammie.

assoc.t: cami, short for camisole, a sleeveless top

e.etymology: From Arabic. Two similar words lie behind it: zakiyya, 'pure, righteous', and dhakiyya, 'intelligent, bright'. Both are written Zakiyah in English.
From Arabic aliya, the feminine of ali, 'high, exalted'. The R&B singer Aaliyah made the name widely known in America in the 1990s, and this spelling drops her final h.

assoc.t: sounds like Aaliyah, the R&B singer (1979-2001)

e.etymology: Occupational surname for a mercer, a dealer in fine cloth, from Old French mercier, 'merchant', from Latin merx, 'goods'.

assoc.t: Mercer, the HR and benefits consulting firm
Mercer University in Georgia; Mercer Island, Washington

e.etymology: A modern coinage in the Kaylin and Kaelyn family, joining the Kay sound to the -lyn ending. The Kei- spellings (Keilyn, Keylin, Keily) are especially used in Spanish-speaking American families.

Geo. was the standard written abbreviation of George in 19th-century records, which is why it appears as a name in the 1880s. George is from Greek georgos, 'farmer', from ge, 'earth', and ergon, 'work'.

assoc.t: geo-, the prefix for earth, as in geography and geology

e.etymology: A modern American coinage joining Ray to the -lon ending of Waylon and Jaylon.
A recent elaboration that sets the Kali or Kalia sound on the -ana ending of Liana and Eliana. It has no established meaning of its own.
A feminine form of Arabic nur, 'light', also written Noura and Noora. An-Nur, 'the Light', is one of the names of God in Islam.
Pet form of Madeleine, 'woman of Magdala' after Mary Magdalene, and of Madison, a surname meaning son of Maud. It is now also given as a full name.

e.meaning: little Giulia; the Italian form of Juliet
e.etymology: Italian diminutive of Giulia (Julia), from the Roman family name Julius. It is the original of Shakespeare's Juliet: the Italian tales he drew on call the Verona heroine Giulietta.

assoc.t: Italian name of Juliet in Romeo and Juliet

e.meaning: from an Italian surname, son of Ermanno (army man)
e.etymology: A respelling of Armani, used as a first name after the Italian fashion house of Giorgio Armani. The surname comes from Armano or Ermanno, Italian forms of the Germanic name Herman, 'army man'.

assoc.t: sounds like Armani, the Italian luxury fashion house

e.etymology: Pet form of Letitia, from Latin laetitia, 'joy, gladness', and of names ending in -lette or -letta such as Colette and Violetta. The usual English spellings are Lettie and Letty.

assoc.t: Letty Ortiz of the Fast & Furious films (spelled Letty)

e.etymology: Hazel with the -ly ending of Paisley and Everly. Hazel is the tree and the light brown eye color, from Old English haesel.
Latin for 'light-bringer', from lux, 'light', and ferre, 'to carry'; the Roman name for the morning star. Christian tradition, reading Isaiah 14:12, made it the name of Satan before his fall.

assoc.t: a name for the Devil in Christian tradition
Lucifer Morningstar, lead of the TV series Lucifer

e.note: Widely understood as the Devil's name; expect strong reactions, and some countries refuse to register it.

e.etymology: A recent coinage that crosses Maisie with Paisley; the -ley ending matches Oakley and Kinsley.

e.meaning: pet form of Dustin; also the word dusty
e.etymology: Pet form of Dustin, a surname probably from Old Norse Thorsteinn, 'Thor's stone'. Dusty is also an old nickname from the English word, traditionally given to men named Miller because millers were covered in flour dust.

assoc.t: Dusty Crophopper, hero of Disney's Planes

e.etymology: A spelling of Mallory, a Norman surname from an Old French word for unlucky. Mallory became a girls' name in the 1980s through Mallory Keaton on the sitcom Family Ties.
namesakes: Malorie Hayes (Sandra Bullock's character in Bird Box)

e.etymology: A spelling of Kori or Corey, an English and Irish surname of uncertain origin that is also used as a short form of Cora and Corinne. It peaked in 2013, when Korie Robertson was on the reality show Duck Dynasty.
From Arabic jamila, the feminine of jamil, 'beautiful'. It entered American use in the 1970s, mainly in African American and Muslim families.
A respelling of Olivia with a y. Olivia is from Latin oliva, 'olive', an early saints' name that Shakespeare popularized in Twelfth Night.
A phonetic spelling of Malik, Arabic for 'king'. Al-Malik, 'the King', is one of the names of God in Islam, and Malik has been common among African Americans since the 1970s.
From Arabic nabil, 'noble, high-born', from the verb nabula, 'to be noble'. Its likeness to the English word noble is a coincidence.
Used mainly in Mexican and Mexican American families, where it spread in the early 1990s; a Mexican telenovela actress performs under the name Amairani. Its origin is not established.
The older Irish form of John, from Latin Ioannes and Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'; Sean arrived later through Norman French. It is often confused with the unrelated Irish name Eoghan.
namesakes: Eoin Colfer (author of the Artemis Fowl books)
e.note: Americans often misread the spelling; it is said like Owen.

e.etymology: A variant of Eliza, the short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, 'my God is an oath'. The added h also makes it look like Elijah, and a few boys receive it as a spelling of that name.
Portuguese, Polish and Romanian form of Louise, the feminine of Louis, from the Frankish name Chlodovech: hlud, 'famous', and wig, 'battle'. It is one of the most popular girls' names in Brazil.

e.meaning: lyric, the words of a song
e.etymology: An elaboration of Lyric, the English word for the words of a song, from Greek lyrikos, 'sung to the lyre'.

assoc.t: prescription nerve-pain drug, heavily advertised on TV

e.note: Lyrica is the brand name of a heavily advertised prescription drug for nerve pain and fibromyalgia.

e.etymology: A coinage that adds the -ston ending of Kingston and Easton to Jax, itself cut from Jaxon, a respelling of Jackson.
